books.section: Topic 7.7 1920s: Innovations in Communication and Technology

primary_sources: Photograph, Frank Conrad's radio station 8XK, July 1920

stimulus.text:
The photograph shows Frank Conrad's radio station 8XK in the garage of his home in Wilkinsburg, Pennsylvania, in July 1920. A wooden table holds coils of wire, glass vacuum tubes, dials, and loose cables.

Background: Conrad's broadcasts led the Westinghouse company to create KDKA in Pittsburgh. KDKA was licensed on October 27, 1920, and on November 2, 1920, it broadcast the returns of the Harding-Cox presidential election.
stimulus.source_note: Photograph, Frank Conrad's radio station 8XK, July 1920, Brown Bros. Photos, public domain (Wikimedia Commons). KDKA facts from the Federal Communications Commission and the Federal Judicial Center.

options.text: the end of all newspaper reporting entirely
options.misconception: Newspapers kept reporting the news after 1920. Radio added a faster channel; it did not end print.

options.text: the start of broadcasting to a mass audience
the invention of the telephone network itself
options.misconception: The telephone network was built in the 1800s. KDKA used telephones to get returns, but it did not invent them.

options.text: the first wartime use of the radio
options.misconception: The broadcast came in peacetime, in 1920, two years after the war ended. Radio's wartime use came earlier and was different.

rationales.A: Newspapers kept reporting the news after 1920. Radio added a faster channel; it did not end print.
rationales.B: Background: KDKA's broadcast reached listeners the same night the votes were counted, before the morning papers. That was the first broadcast to a mass audience.
rationales.C: The telephone network was built in the 1800s. KDKA used telephones to get returns, but it did not invent them.
rationales.D: The broadcast came in peacetime, in 1920, two years after the war ended. Radio's wartime use came earlier and was different.
rationales.general:
1. Note the date: November 2, 1920, the night of the presidential election.
2. Note the audience: listeners heard the returns the same night, before the morning papers.
3. Name the moment: the first broadcast aimed at a mass audience, not at one receiver.
4. Note what changed: news could now reach listeners the night it happened, not the next morning.
Remember: a first broadcast counts when it speaks to many listeners at once.
